title: Harvey's headcount surged sixfold in a single year—trust, not process, sustains this pace
dek: In one year, Harvey's valuation leapt from $30 billion to $110 billion, and headcount from 300+ to nearly 2,000. Yet the VP of Talent credits this pace not to new process, but to founders' trust and employee autonomy that have never been constrained.
why: Explains the specific mechanics of how a four-year-old company hires a thousand people in a year without fragmenting—essential for founders and HR leaders scaling teams rapidly. The opening pleasantries can be skipped.
who: For founders, HR leads, and early employees scaling rapidly and relying on values and trust to maintain efficiency in the absence of mature processes.
skip: The first two minutes covering the company's birthday celebration and team atmosphere pleasantries.

points.h: Harvey's headcount surged sixfold in a single year
points.body: Maggie joined just one year ago when employee numbers were in the 300s, yet Harvey has added over 1,000 new hires and expects to approach 2,000 by year-end. The critical insight: over 70% of the current staff joined after January 1 this year, meaning many recruiting managers, recruiters, and new hires themselves are new to the company. They're figuring out as they work what actually works in Harvey's culture, rather than importing playbooks from previous employers.

points.h: Harvey ships in a month what most companies take a quarter to deliver
points.body: Maggie emphasizes that Harvey's pace functions as a filtering mechanism. Even people who felt their prior company moved fast discover Harvey operates on a completely different scale. Most new hires were successful in their previous fields and accustomed to getting things right, but Harvey requires letting go of ‘must be first’ thinking and accepting a higher error rate. The focus shifts to rapid failure and rapid correction rather than getting it perfect the first time.

points.h: Founders eliminate approval chains and stay directly engaged in operations
points.body: Maggie describes what makes founders Winston and Gabe distinctive: they combine strategic foresight with deep involvement in daily execution details. Harvey isn't the kind of company where you submit a deck, wait eight weeks, and eventually see executives—staff can reach Winston or Gabe directly on Slack and get near-instant responses. This accessibility cascaded through the entire leadership team, including later hires like COO and CISO, shaping how they approach daily work.

points.h: Harvey's adolescent stage—between startup chaos and corporate maturity—filters candidates
points.body: Maggie characterizes Harvey as operating in ‘adolescence’—neither the pre-PMF startup with fuzzy role boundaries nor a mature corporation running like clockwork. This in-between state naturally filters people: some want more structure and stability, others prefer earlier-stage chaos. The recruiting team's job is to make the interview experience reflect the actual working state as closely as possible, letting candidates judge for themselves whether they want to stay.

points.h: Three core values sustain speed without waiting for consensus
points.body: Every candidate interviews around three core values: Simplicity, Decisiveness, and ‘Jobs not finished.’ Decisiveness means better to err than over-analyze—decisions aren't made by waiting for 300 people to agree. Simplicity means not over-building; ship first and gather feedback. ‘Jobs not finished’ demands humility, acknowledging that current approaches could always be better. Together, these enable people who are accustomed to perfectionism to release that grip.

points.h: As scale increased, founders chose to preserve trust over control
points.body: Winston said in an internal founder Q&A that what he most wanted to preserve during scaling was trust. Maggie believes this trust in staff translates directly to autonomy for front-line employees: no multi-level approvals, no excessive oversight. That's what allows Harvey to continue hiring a thousand people, making mistakes, and experimenting at its current pace. Even with only four years of history, this trust has never been tightened.

points.h: Legal expertise outweighs pure AI backgrounds in hiring
points.body: Maggie reminds candidates that transforming legal is completely different from transforming customer service, building AI harnesses, or building models—even though Harvey now builds its own models. The company has many current or former practicing lawyers scattered across product (applied legal researcher), innovation partnerships (legal innovation partner), and sales (legal engineer). Interest in and respect for the legal industry itself is what distinguishes Harvey from companies like Anthropic, OpenAI, 11 Labs, and Sierra. Candidates need to think this through before deciding to join.

points.h: Judgment is the hardest quality to assess, yet determines who succeeds
points.body: In an environment of high autonomy and rapid decisions, the most critical but hardest-to-evaluate quality is judgment: knowing when to loop in the right person before you hit send, rather than gathering 20 people for a meeting or going completely solo. Maggie describes it as a voice in the back of your head. It's precisely this judgment that lets employees with substantial autonomy maintain the company's trust in them.
